pages.text: T. rex had lips, upending its enduring pop culture image | National Geographic Premium SCIENCE ​ T. rex had lips, upending its enduring pop culture image Whether carnivorous dinosaurs had lips has long been the stuff of paleo-debate. A new study finds evidence that flesh covered the predators’ teeth. Tyrannosaurus rex and other carnivorous dinosaurs likely had soft tissue that covered their sharp teeth, as seen in this illustration. Lips would have kept their teeth moist and protected—and ready to attack prey. Illustration by Mark P. Witton By Riley Black Published March 30, 2023 • 6 min read The fearsome jaws of Tyrannosaurus are famous. In museum halls, paleo art, and even feature films such as Jurassic Park , the Cretaceous carnivore has traditionally been depicted with banana-size fangs and a sinister grin. But paleontologists have now discovered that the living animal did not have a sharp-toothed smirk— T. rex , as well as many other carnivorous dinosaurs, had lips. Reported today in Science , a multi-institution team of paleontologists propose that carnivorous dinosaurs like T. rex and Allosaurus had fleshy lips covering their teeth, much as modern-day lizards do. The hypothesis will likely alter both the public image of dinosaurs as well as how paleontologists study the ways these terrible lizards fed. ( Time to Slay the T. rex Scavenger “Debate”) The new research got its start as discussions between co-authors Thomas Cullen , Kirstin Brink , and Derek Larson while all three were graduate students at the University of Toronto. pages.description: The formidable Tyrannosaurus rex had nothing to fear—except possibly its own kind, gnawed fossil bones suggest.
pages.text: T. Rex Was a Cannibal, Bone Gashes Suggest | National Geographic Tooth gouges on this 65-million-year-old T. rex toe bone could have been made only by another T. rex. Diagram courtesy Nicholas Longrich, Yale University T. Rex Was a Cannibal, Bone Gashes Suggest Mighty predators may have attacked kin or scavenged corpses. By Brian Handwerk Published October 15, 2010 • 3 min read The formidable Tyrannosaurus rex likely had nothing to fear—except possibly its own kind, a new study suggests. Paleontologist Nick Longrich of Yale University was examining dinosaur bones found in Montana when he noticed large gouges in bones that had yet to be indentifiied. The gouges had to have been made by a large carnivore, he said, and when the mystery fossils were deposited 65 million years ago, T. rex was the only North American carnivore large and toothy enough to make such marks. But the seemingly routine find took a macabre turn when Longrich discovered one of the bitten bones belonged to a T. rex —making it apparent evidence of cannibalism. This toe bone "has giant theropod bite marks, and the only one there [at that time] was T. rex ," he said. "There was really no other conclusion I could come to." (Related: "Tiny T. rex Ancestors Achieved World Domination." ) Further analysis in several fossil collections turned up three more similarly bitten T. rex bones. Longrich and colleagues speculate the giant predators may have engaged in cannibalism with some regularity—but it's unknown whether the dinosaurs fought to the death or simply scavenged T. rex corpses. A Paris railway station on a miserable, rainy January night feels worlds away from sunny alpine slopes and high-altitude soft powder. But vintage train carriages emblazoned with ‘Les Arcs’, ‘La Plagne’, ‘Tignes’, ‘Meribel’ and ‘Val d’Isere’ get my adrenaline flowing. At the belle époque-style Gare de Lyon, Guillaume de Marcillac, co-founder and CEO of Pegasus Trains, is greeting passengers about to board the sleeper train. He explains that by repurposing “elderly” train stock, his company offers travellers “a credible, low-impact alternative to flying or driving to their winter sport destination”. The train, chartered by UK tour operator Travelski for the 2025-26 winter season, is the first sleeper service to the Alps in nine years — and there are plans for it to run for winters to come. Close TaoEngine's Diary 【有时间就来写写枞阳的一些事情】关于康居路 Posted by TaoEngine on 15 July 2026 in Chinese (China) (‪中文(中国大陆)‬) . osm的小伙伴们大家好，今天我无意中发现了osm可以写日记然后放在自己的首页中。有的小伙伴分析地区编辑完完整度，有的教大家正确使用地图标签。虽然我注册有三年多了但是论辈分还是个小老弟😂，那我就写写我比较擅长的东西，欸要不我就写写有关家乡的一些事好了哈 关于康居路 枞阳县枞阳镇旗山社区邻近枞阳县人民医院、银塘花苑与银塘星城这三个区域中间有一条三级道路，道路有花坛阻拦，两条单行道形式，双向四车道（高峰期两车道因为两边可以停车） 这条道路的命名其实非常迷，枞阳县地图与天地图将其命名为健康路，而枞阳县ZY-02银塘行政区规划文件与地名信息系统将其命名为康居路（商业地图通常采用后者）。这条路到底叫康居路还是健康路？ 其实我住的地方离这条路不远，所以经常在傍晚散步时走这条路。根据我的见解以及查阅对应文件的思路，这条路现阶段应该还是命名为康居路为好，至少26年8月之前还是得叫它康居路 1. 根据路灯管理局的路灯标签判断 26年初，县里开展《城市生命线》安全设备部署工作，在大街小巷安装了监测设备，同时县里也提及同日设立路灯管理所。随即4月份县里的每个路灯都贴上了标签，其中这条路的路灯被贴上康居路标签。这项工作是领先于枞阳县地图的制作的，可以认定当前这条道路仍为康居路 2. 根据枞阳县ZY-02银塘行政区规划文件中康居小区存在与否判断 在枞阳县地图中，康居路并未消失而是跑到了旗山小学与中海山水城的区域中间，而它的命名依据是因为附近有个小区名为康居山庄。但是无论是在枞阳县ZY-02银塘行政区规划文件中，还是在旗山社区服务站点地图中，这个不是小区，是银塘村的回迁房，经简单查阅县政府公开文档初步确认区域名为银塘安置地。真正现存的“康居山庄”在妇幼保健院旁边，不过叫康居家园。当然不排除小区未来改名的情况 其次那条路虽然在路灯管理所的标签、附近停车场名称以及路牌中没有给出详细名称，但是在枞阳县ZY-02银塘行政区规划文件中，这条路被命名为安置地路。鉴于规划文件的审图号较枞阳县地图较新，该未分级道路我建议命名为安置地路，而保留原先的康居路命名位置 为啥要写这条路 上次有个过于热心的小伙伴将康居路所在道路标为健康路（与此同时他还把旗山路标为莲城路，而莲城路是天地图的一处过时标记，我有时间在下一次日记里说），希望我的笔记能在我没时间贡献枞阳的时候，给其他人一些有理可循的参考（与此同时我也会夹带一些私货介绍枞阳有什么有意思的地方，比如枞阳中学占据的地方曾经有个自然村叫答咀村，这个村的来历可神奇了，另开一个新坑），望大家多多关照👋 Location: 殷家老屋, 枞阳县, 枞阳镇, 枞阳县, 铜陵市, 安徽省, 246700, 中国 Discussion Comment from TaoEngine on 18 November 2026 at 04:59 打脸了，旗山小学那条路今天立牌子了😭就是康居路，马上改 Leave a comment Log in to leave a comment

pages.text: Technical Documentation of Intermediate Tables for Improved Imputation of Tax Credits Technical Documentation of Intermediate Tables for Improved Imputation of Tax Credits Skip Navigation Within Census Bureau Library Technical Documentation of Intermediate Tables for Improved Imputation of Tax Credits January 2025 Written by: Adam Bee and Matthew Unrath Working Paper Number: SEHSD-WP2024-32 Introduction This technical documentation describes a new data release that will aid users of the Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC) tax variables. Using linked survey and administrative data, we produce tabulations of several intermediate imputation targets (e.g., filing rates, shares by filing status, numbers of dependents claimed, eligibility for key tax credits) for an array of tax unit types in the 2019 CPS ASEC. Data users can use these tables to improve imputations of tax variables in the public-use 2019 CPS ASEC. However, it is important to note that these intermediate values do not represent sample estimates of U.S. population characteristics. Technology Commercialization Fund The Technology Commercialization Fund (TCF) is a U.S. Department of Energy program that helps move innovations developed at DOE National Laboratories, plants, and sites into the marketplace. Established by Congress in the Energy Policy Act of 2005, TCF invests millions of dollars each year to bridge the gap between research and commercial application. The program supports partnerships between DOE facilities and industry, universities, and other organizations to advance technologies with strong market potential. By sharing costs with private and public partners, TCF strengthens the lab-to-market pipeline, fosters collaboration, and ensures that federally funded research delivers tangible benefits to the nation’s economy and energy security. pages.text: Teesside conservationists search for European eels in River Tees Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Conservationists searching for large river eels 8 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Tom Burgess North East and Cumbria Tees Rivers Trust Tees Rivers Trust workers have been tagging eels to track their downstream migration Conservationists have spent summer and autumn searching for critically endangered eels to tag as they begin their downstream migration. The Tees Rivers Trust have found 12 large eels by fyke netting, a method of catching eels with a cylindrical net, around the River Tees catchment. The team managed to electronically tag 10 of them and the largest was 60cm (23ins) in length and weighted 435g (0.9lbs). Project manager Ellie Ward said the eels caught this year were not as large as usual and were "harder to catch". The team has been searching for "silver" eels which have finished maturing and are preparing to head back out to the Sargasso Sea near Bermuda. Ward said: "European eels start to migrate downstream during autumn and winter, when river discharges increase. "We suspect that low flows in summer that have continued into autumn have contributed to low catch rates so far this year." 'Mystery' species The Eels of Steel project is funded by Natural England and the Tees Rivers Trust has been conducting the research alongside Hull University. Los gastos calificados son cantidades que usted pagó o en los que incurrió por participar en cursos de desarrollo profesional, libros, artículos escolares, equipo relacionado con la informática (incluyendo software y servicios relacionados), otro equipo y materiales suplementarios que utiliza en el aula. Para los cursos de salud o educación física, los gastos de artículos escolares deben ser por suministros relacionados con el atletismo. Get our Newsletter! Like many birds, domestic turkeys, including this group at the Smithsonian's National Zoo in Washington, D.C., are social animals. Smithsonian/Brett Kuxhausen 1. Humans have been raising turkeys for thousands of years. Although indigenous peoples in North America have hunted wild turkeys since the end of the last Ice Age, the animals were first domesticated in Mexico around 2,000 years ago. Dinner wasn’t the original goal: archaeological evidence suggests turkeys were initially kept so their feathers could be used in clothing and ceremonial regalia. By A.D. 500, people were raising turkeys in what is now the United States too, judging by archaeological remains from caves in Arizona and New Mexico. Even so, those weren’t the birds that English settlers ate in the Thirteen Colonies. The domestic turkey descends from a southern Mexican bird that the Spanish took home in the 1500s. The birds then spread through Europe, and colonists brought them back across the Atlantic. The bird’s English name may reflect this long-distance trade: turkeys are thought to have reached England along winding trading routes that first passed through the country of Turkey. 2. All adults and pregnant women should get tested for hepatitis B. People with ongoing risk need periodic testing. You can find out if you have hepatitis B through a blood test. Why get tested Many people with hepatitis B do not look or feel sick, so testing is the only way to know if you are infected. It's important to get tested for hepatitis B, so that if you are infected you can get medical care and avoid spreading the virus to others. Chronic, or long-term, hepatitis B can cause serious health problems, including liver damage, liver cancer, liver failure, and even death. Tetanus: Causes and How It Spreads For Everyone Sept. 10, 2026 Español Key points Tetanus spores from the environment enter the body through cuts or wounds. Tetanus doesn't spread from person to person. It is possible to have tetanus infection more than once. Prevent tetanus by staying up to date with vaccinations and seeking appropriate care after a wound. Causes Bacteria live in the environment Spores of Clostridium tetani are common in the environment, including soil, dust, and manure. The spores develop into bacteria when they enter the body. Common exposures The spores can get into someone's body through broken skin, usually through injuries. pages.description: Scientists call the events permafrost detachment slides. Instead of thawing from the top down, these landslides seem to originate from a weakened base
pages.text: Thawing Permafrost May Have Created a New Type of Landslide, Which Could Become More Common as the World Warms Skip to main content A scar left by the 2018 Redstone River permafrost landslide, one of the two events investigated in the new study. Adapted from J. M. Young et al., Geophysical Research Letters , 2026 In 2017 and 2018, a pair of strange landslides moved huge masses of rock and dirt in Canada’s Northwest Territories. The events occurred in the central Mackenzie Valley, and one of them even dammed a river and created a lake . The two natural disasters are part of a new class of landslides scientists are calling “permafrost detachment slides” in a study published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters in September. They may have been partially triggered by severe wildfires that occurred in 1995, which destabilized the ground and allowed the base of the permafrost to thaw. What’s more, these events may become more common as the planet continues to warm. “It’s a very dramatic manifestation of the changing climate,” says study co-author Joseph Young , a geoscientist who conducted the work at the University of Alberta in Canada, to Matt Simon at Grist . “They’ve only started happening in the last 10, 15 years, and it’s a very drastic and abrupt change in the landscape.” Young and his colleagues began the study after seeing something strange in the Northwest Territories in 2019. While conducting field research, they spotted large landslide scars in valleys that they knew were stable permafrost , or permanently frozen earth, reports Stephanie Pappas for Live Science

Learn about other national symbols. History of the American flag The flag of the United States is a symbol of freedom before which Americans recite the pledge of allegiance . The flag's 13 red and white stripes represent the 13 original colonies. Its 50 white stars on a blue background represent the 50 states. Each of the colors on the flag has a meaning: Red: valor and bravery White: purity and innocence Blue: vigilance, perseverance, and justice A star is added to the flag when a new state joins the United States. The flag was last modified on July 4, 1960, when Hawaii was incorporated as a state. Learn more about the evolution of the American flag and its earlier designs. How to raise the flag Follow these guidelines to properly display the American flag [PDF, 162KB]. When to fly the flag at half-staff The American flag flies at half-staff or at half-mast when the country or a state is in mourning. The president, a state governor, or the mayor of the District of Columbia can order flags to fly at half-staff. In the foothills, access routes to the mines ran through an area called Nok. Over the years, with the exploitation of the mines and the local people who overwhelmingly provided the labor force, numerous fragments of ancient pottery came to light but were largely ignored. The continent of North America has been inhabited by humans for at least 16,500 years. As early as the 1500s, early settlers and European thinkers were interested in discovering how humans had come to populate North and South America. One theory suggested the migration of Norsemen across Greenland into North America. Another theory proposed the island of Atlantis as the origins of human life in the New World. Yet another idea proposed that the inhabitants had generated out of mud. However, by the early 1800s, scientists and theorists began discussing the possibility of a land bridge that had spanned between Asia and North America thousands of years ago. Scarred skulls, scraped ground, and fossilized trackways suggest adult tyrannosaurs lived largely solitary lives, like modern big cats, but also gathered in communal display arenas to woo potential mates. Before the discovery of “Sue,” “Stan,” “Scotty,” and many other famous skeletons of Earth’s last great carnivorous dinosaur, AMNH 5027 was the icon. pages.text: The deadly race to decipher Maya hieroglyphs | National Geographic By George E. Stuart Photographs by Otis Imboden Published March 6, 2026 This story originally published in the December 1975 issue of National Geographic magazine. See more digitized stories from our archives here . Murder and Maya hieroglyphs make an unlikely combination, but the two came together one evening several years ago, deep in the rain forest of northern Guatemala. It happened at La Naya, soon after Scotsman Ian Graham and his party had arrived to draw and photograph inscriptions that had been reported at the remote ruin. They found much more than they bargained for. "I never thought Maya archeology would be that dangerous," Ian told me when I visited him at Harvard University's Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology, "but I sometimes feel fortunate to be alive. The looters are quite serious about their business." At La Naya, Ian and his group had unwittingly interrupted a gang of men engaged in cutting apart an ancient stone monument. Later, as the archeologists were setting up camp, shots rang out and Pedro Arturo Sierra, one of Ian's assistants, fell dying. The shooting was an isolated incident. But looting still occurs frequently enough to deprive us of priceless knowledge of the fascinating ancient Maya civilization. At Naranjo, a site near the Guatemala-Belize border, half the 40 known monuments have been attacked. By Nicholas St. Fleur Published July 27, 2026 Were Neanderthals Europe’s first painters? And did they use cave walls as their canvases? Scientists long thought that Homo sapiens —like us—were the only human species capable of creating artwork in caves. But in recent years, suspiciously old rock art found in caves throughout Spain, like the 65,000-year-old red lines in the Cave of La Pasiega , has led some to wonder if our extinct cousins were the artists instead. The findings left many experts wondering if our extinct cousins were the artists behind these prehistoric masterpieces. Now, researchers are hoping ancient DNA will hold the answer.
